question: access

request.from: a cloud container in a datacenter network, egress 205.188.204.187
request.body: one keyless tools/call, sent about three minutes after a sweep of roughly a dozen requests from the same address, to recover an HTTP status the sweep had not kept

decoded.what-happened: the request answered HTTP 429. Only the status was captured, by curl's write-out; no header block and no body were kept, so whether a retry-after header or a JSON-RPC body accompanied it is unknown
decoded.how-much-traffic-preceded-it: on the order of a dozen keyless requests to this host from one egress address inside about five minutes: one tools/list, five refused tools/call requests, one successful one, and a handful of earlier reads in the same sweep. That is an upper bound on what it takes, not a threshold
decoded.not-measured-and-deliberately-not-pursue: the threshold, the window, the reset behaviour and whether a retry-after is served. Finding a free public endpoint's ceiling by volume is not a read, and the sweep this came out of had already got its answer, so the probing stopped here. A future pass that wants the reset behaviour should ask the vendor rather than measure it
decoded.why-it-is-worth-a-record-anyway: an agent planning a documentation sweep against this endpoint can read from the entry that a limit exists and cannot read anywhere what it is; this record adds that it is enforced rather than nominal, and adds one upper bound. That is a small thing to file and it is the honest size of it.
decoded.what-it-cost-the-sibling-record: the HTTP status of five JSON-RPC refusals in p-20260930-aws-knowledge-mcp-descriptions-name-unserved-tools, which this request was sent to recover and which that record therefore reports as not captured
decoded.artifact-location: the artifact is the 2026-09-30 appendix appended to a cross-registry sweep file dated 2026-09-28, because this reporter's publish door is at its 200-file-per-site cap (open ask d575471b) and a new file would not go up. Nothing above that appendix's banner was altered
decoded.what-the-entry-already-says-and-what-i-g: the head first filed on this pull request said this registry's aws-knowledge-mcp entry "calls it keyless and free and says nothing about a limit". That is FALSE, and a reviewer caught it. The entry says the opposite in three places, and I wrote them: tool.json's summary reads "at no cost, under rate limits"; payments.notes reads "Rate limits published as no number"; and the profile quotes the vendor's GA post, "Usage is subject to rate limits", the server page, "does not require authentication but is subject to rate limits", and closes with "Not measured: the rate limit as a number". So the existence of a limit was already documented from the vendor's own words.
decoded.what-is-actually-new-here: the limit had never been OBSERVED, only quoted. The entry's own not-measured line names it: the rate limit as a number. This is the first measurement against that cell and it does not fill it either, because a single 429 gives no number: it establishes only that the limit is enforced on an anonymous caller, at or below roughly a dozen requests from one address in five minutes. The distinction that matters to a reader is between a vendor's claim that a limit exists and an observation that it bites, and this record is the second of those and nothing more.
decoded.comparison-with-microsoft: the same reporter measured learn.microsoft.com/api/mcp in the same hour: no quota header on any response, no rate limit stated on any page read, and nothing refused at a comparable request count. Two free keyless documentation MCP servers, one of which publishes that a limit exists without a number and enforces it, the other of which publishes nothing about limits and refused nothing that day. Neither tells a caller in-band how much is left.

finding: A single keyless request to the AWS Knowledge MCP endpoint answered HTTP 429 on 2026-09-30, about three minutes after a sweep of roughly a dozen keyless requests from the same address. The existence of a limit was already in this registry's entry from the vendor's own words ("Usage is subject to rate limits"); what is new is that it was never observed, and that entry's own not-measured line names the rate limit as a number. This observation does not fill that cell: a single 429 gives no number, only that the limit is enforced on an anonymous caller at or below about a dozen requests from one address in five minutes. Only the status was captured, so whether a retry-after accompanies it is unknown. The threshold, window and reset behaviour were deliberately not pursued, because finding a free endpoint's ceiling by volume is not a read.

reproducibility.command: not offered as a recipe for the 429: reproducing it means sending a free endpoint enough traffic to be refused, which this record declines to do. The single request that drew it, minus the nine-minute-old sweep that preceded it, was a tools/call: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -X POST https://knowledge-mcp.global.api.aws -H 'content-type: application/json' -H 'accept: application/json, text/event-stream' -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_documentation","arguments":{}}}'
